title: The Effectiveness of Debriefing on the Mental Health of Rescue Teams: A Systematic Review
content: Rescue teams and emergency services face high levels of mental health problems due to their frequent exposure to traumatic situations. Although post-incident psychosocial support interventions, such as debriefing, are widely implemented, their effectiveness in preventing disorders such as PTSD or depression remains uncertain. This systematic review, conducted within the framework of the working group “Debriefing and Psychological Support to Rescue Teams” of the University of Zaragoza, analyzes the effectiveness of debriefing in military, emergency, and health personnel. Following PRISMA guidelines and Cochrane methodology, 371 studies were identified, of which 6 met the inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the review. The methodological assessment with the PEDro scale showed that one study was of high quality, four were of acceptable quality, and two had deficiencies. Although some interventions, such as the “512 PIM”, offered promising results in reducing PTSD and anxiety symptoms, overall, the evidence on the effectiveness of debriefing was limited and inconsistent. In addition, adverse effects such as increased alcohol consumption were observed in certain groups. No specific effects have been studied in mountain rescue teams. We found limited evidence on the effectiveness of post-incident psychosocial interventions in rescue and emergency teams. More high-quality studies are urgently needed to understand better how to prevent the development of trauma-related disorders after exposure to traumatic events.
